Official Scope + Assigned Resources

1. Describe the pathogenesis of vascular access-site infections and list the common organisms involved.
2. Provide a reasonable management strategy for vascular access-site infections caused by common and problem organisms.
3. Outline the pathogenesis, diagnosis, and treatment of infected burn wounds.
4. Recognize common pathogens and disease presentations associated with defects in WBC function, cell-mediated immunity, humoral immunity, and splenic dysfunction.
Assigned resources
ScholarRx · Health care–associated infectionsScholarRx · Phagocyte dysfunction
Best mental map: ask which host defense is missing. Barrier breach → catheter/burn flora. CMI → intracellular/opportunistic patterns. Humoral or spleen → encapsulated bacteria. Phagocyte dysfunction → catalase-positive organisms; diabetes/DKA → invasive mucormycosis pattern in this deck.

Slides 3–14 · Vascular Access-Site Infection

Why the catheter matters

A long-term vascular device breaches a physical barrier. The deck emphasizes Gram-positive cocci as the most common organisms, especially coagulase-negative staphylococci.

Local clues

Erythema, warmth, tenderness, and induration at the access site raise concern. The harder question is whether the device is actually the source of bacteremia.

Slide 7. When the catheter remains in place, Fisher gives three diagnostic strategies: simultaneous quantitative blood cultures, differential time to positivity, and acridine-orange WBC cytospin.

Catheter removed: culture the device

Roll-plate method
>15 colonies is the deck’s threshold.
Sonication method
After sonication/dilution, >100 colonies is shown as the threshold.

Management is organism + severity dependent

Deck scenarioManagement taught
Coagulase-negative staph, patient not acutely illRemoval gives faster response/fewer relapses. Antimicrobial options shown: MSSA → nafcillin; MRSA → vancomycin or ceftaroline; deck gives 5–7 days in the removal scenario.
Coagulase-negative staph, catheter salvageVancomycin antibiotic-lock 5 mg/mL for 7–14 days; if blood cultures are positive, add IV vancomycin for 7–14 days.
S. aureus bacteremia / acutely illRemove catheter; MSSA → nafcillin, MRSA → vancomycin or ceftaroline; rule out endocarditis and metastatic abscess; deck gives 4–6 weeks.
Gram-negative bacillary catheter infectionRemove catheter; carbapenem initially, then de-escalate after cultures; deck gives 14 days.
Candida catheter infectionRemove catheter; echinocandin or fluconazole; deck gives 14 days after last positive culture.
Slide 13. The deck treats S. aureus catheter-associated bloodstream infection as the high-risk pattern: remove the line, look for endocarditis/metastatic abscess, and use prolonged therapy.

Slides 15–21 · Burn-Wound Infection

Superficial burn
Cool with tap water. No topical antibiotics. No dressing needed.
Superficial partial-thickness
Colonization is frequent. Mild cleansing; topical antimicrobial; non-adherent dressing; leave blister intact when possible.
Deep partial/full-thickness
The deck shifts to invasive infection/sepsis logic with wound biopsy burden and systemic findings.
Slide 19. Deep-partial/full-thickness burn pathogens emphasized by Fisher: staphylococci (with >50% MRSA noted), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter baumannii. The slide uses >105 bacteria/g tissue as the infection threshold.
Burn sepsis treatment from the deck: early excision (usually 24–72 h, within 5 days) down to fascia with cultures + empiric coverage for MRSA and Gram-negative rods using an anti-pseudomonal β-lactam + vancomycin, then cover the excised area with mesh dressing.
Slide 21. Fisher’s burn-sepsis management sequence: early excision/cultures plus empiric MRSA + GNR coverage.

Slides 22–26 · Defects in Cell-Mediated Immunity

The deck groups primary immune disorders, malignancy, HIV infection, and iatrogenic immunosuppression under CMI defects, then teaches transplant-associated examples.

CMV after renal transplant

Classic syndrome in the deck: fever/malaise about two months after transplant with mild transaminitis, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia. Diagnosis shown: CMV DNA by quantitative NAT. Treatment shown: mild → valganciclovir; severe → IV ganciclovir.

Miliary TB

For prolonged fever, chills/sweats, weight loss, weakness, and cough after renal transplant, the deck uses miliary TB as the pattern-recognition example.

Slide 23. CMV syndrome after renal transplantation: fever, mild liver-enzyme elevation, leukopenia/thrombocytopenia, and CMV DNA by QNAT.
Slide 26. CMI-defect CNS pattern: cryptococcal meningitis. The deck shows liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine followed by fluconazole.

Slides 27–28 · Humoral Immunity

Acquired causes shown

Multiple myeloma and B-cell lymphoma → defective immunoglobulin. Protein-losing enteropathy and nephrotic syndrome → immunoglobulin loss.

Pathogen pattern

The deck’s central association is encapsulated bacteria, particularly Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae.

Faculty-question cue: untreated multiple myeloma + bacterial pneumonia → the deck points to pneumococcus, so expect Gram-positive diplococci.

Slides 29–30 · Phagocytic Defects

Slide 29. Chronic granulomatous disease: defective NADPH oxidase → no respiratory burst / oxygen metabolites. The slide emphasizes susceptibility to catalase-positive organisms.
Ozzy found the phagocyte section 🐾 His recall check: CGD = NADPH oxidase defect → no respiratory burst → catalase-positive organism risk.
Slide 30. Diabetic ketoacidosis pattern: severe maxillary pain, nasal congestion, blurred vision, and Rhizopus/Rhizomucor/Mucor. Fisher links low pH to increased available iron and shows emergent surgery + liposomal amphotericin B.

Slide 31 · Splenic Dysfunction

Slide 31. Sickle-cell functional asplenia is paired with fulminant infection by encapsulated bacteria: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and N. meningitidis. Fisher notes very high early mortality and that vaccines are protective.
Humoral vs spleen shortcut: both point you toward encapsulated bacteria. The spleen slide broadens the core set to S. pneumoniae + H. influenzae + N. meningitidis.

Slides 32–40 · Faculty Question Anchors

Q32. Adult with sickle-cell functional asplenia: organism risk among listed options?
Anchor: Haemophilus influenzae.
Q33. Tunneled catheter with exit-site infection: statistically most likely organism?
Anchor: Staphylococcus epidermidis.
Q34. CGD child with pneumonia and lung abscess: most likely listed organism?
Anchor: Staphylococcus aureus.
Q35. Untreated multiple myeloma + pneumonia: expected sputum morphology?
Anchor: Gram-positive diplococci → pneumococcus.
Q36. Two months after renal transplant with fever/malaise and no localizing source?
Anchor: CMV.
Q37. Limited-access patient with S. epidermidis catheter bacteremia, otherwise stable?
Deck logic: catheter salvage with IV therapy plus antibiotic-lock therapy for about 2 weeks.
Q38. Catheter bloodstream infection with Candida parapsilosis?
Deck logic: remove catheter + systemic antifungal; 14 days after the last positive culture.
Q39. Prior splenectomy + fulminant fever, altered mental status, petechiae/purpura?
Anchor: Neisseria meningitidis.
Q40. Most common organism causing CNS infection following solid-organ transplant among listed choices?
Anchor taught immediately before the questions: Cryptococcus neoformans.

Last 60 Seconds

Catheter = Gram+ cocci, especially coagulase-negative staph · S. aureus catheter bacteremia = remove line + search for endocarditis/metastatic infection · Candida catheter infection = remove + antifungal · deep burn infection = staph/MRSA + Pseudomonas + Acinetobacter; >105/g on the deck · burn sepsis = early excision + anti-pseudomonal β-lactam + vanco · transplant CMI = CMV / TB / Crypto patterns · humoral + asplenia = encapsulated bacteria · CGD = NADPH oxidase, catalase+ organisms · DKA + facial pain = mucor → surgery + liposomal amphotericin B.
